input: Draft a family technology usage agreement

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The ages and number of children drastically change the rules — screen time limits, content restrictions, and tone differ between a 6-year-old and a 16-year-old.
Technology covers a huge range — smartphones, gaming consoles, social media, streaming, school devices — knowing which are in or out shapes the entire document.
Whether this is for everyday home use, also covers school nights vs. weekends, or extends to use at grandparents' homes affects which rules need to be written.
Key hard limits like bedtime cut-offs, total daily hours, or device-free zones (dinner table, bedrooms) are the backbone of the agreement and must be defined.
The tone — fun and collaborative vs. firm and rule-focused — determines whether the agreement reads like a family contract everyone signed together or a parent-set policy.
Knowing whether the goal is to reduce conflict, build healthy habits, set safety guardrails, or all three determines which sections to emphasise.
The format — a printable one-page document, a detailed multi-section contract, or a simple checklist — determines length, layout, and how it will actually be used.

gold.taskTitle: Draft a Family Technology Usage Agreement
gold.taskDescription: Write a shared agreement that sets rules and expectations for how technology is used within the family.

questions.title: What are the ages of the children this covers?
questions.description: Understanding the age range of the children involved determines the appropriate rules, language, and level of restriction in the agreement.

questions.title: Which devices or platforms should the agreement cover?
questions.description: Clarifying whether this covers smartphones, gaming consoles, social media, streaming services, school-issued devices, or all of the above defines the scope of the document.

questions.title: Does it apply differently on school nights versus weekends?
questions.description: Knowing whether rules vary by day type or location (home, away, travel) determines how many distinct rule sets need to be written.

questions.title: Are there any non-negotiable limits already decided on?
questions.description: Hard limits like no devices at dinner, phones off at 9pm, or a two-hour daily cap are the structural backbone of the agreement and should be captured early.

questions.title: Should the tone feel like a family pact or a parent-set rule?
questions.description: Whether the agreement is framed as something everyone co-created together or as a policy set by parents shapes the language, format, and how it will be received.

questions.title: What is the main problem this agreement is meant to solve?
questions.description: Knowing the primary goal — reducing screen-time arguments, ensuring online safety, building healthy habits, or setting clear consequences — determines which sections to prioritise.

questions.title: What format should the final document be in?
questions.description: Determining whether the output should be a printable one-page summary, a detailed multi-section contract with signature lines, or a simple checklist affects length and layout.
